text:
The Penguins arrive in Nashville as a team being talked about in the past tense. Erik Karlsson has been in 30 headlines in two weeks, almost all of them about where he goes next, and the reporting now covers Evgeni Malkin and Kris Letang too. Rickard Rakell has already used his no-trade list to block a move to Chicago, per Yahoo Sports and WPXI. NHL.com's headline on Sidney Crosby this week said he knows the Penguins need a turnaround to keep the veteran core intact. At 16 points and an 11% playoff chance by our numbers, the clock on that turnaround is loud.

The frustrating part for Pittsburgh is that the hockey has been better than the record. They have 52% of the five-on-five expected goals (the quality of the chances), yet their goal difference sits at -13 on -3.7 expected, and finishing has cost them about eight goals. The recent stretch is harder to excuse: they lost the chance battle in four of the last five. Malkin (upper body) and Bryan Rust are out, and Ben Kindel has climbed to about 19 minutes a night in their place. Sergei Murashov gets the net over Arturs Silovs, carrying a .893 save percentage across eight games.

Nashville comes home after five on the road, the back half of which went sideways. A seven-game winning streak ended in San Jose, and then Minnesota put seven on them. Juuse Saros is the reason the streak existed: .943 over his last five starts, nearly ten goals saved above expected on the season, and his name at the top of Vezina rankings after a minus-10 season last year. Steven Stamkos brings a four-game point streak, though his goals have outrun his chances. Ryan O'Reilly left practice early this week, per Yahoo Sports, so his status is worth checking at warmups.

Our numbers make it close, 3.52 expected goals for Nashville to 3.25 for Pittsburgh. We'd watch Ross Colton, our sleeper: a fourth-liner with 3.5 expected goals in his last ten games, at 18% to score.
headline: The Penguins sell, and Saros keeps saving
